title: Spain's midfield masterclass sinks Germany
summary: A Pedri double and Yamal's second-half assist handed Spain a 2-0 victory over Germany, with La Roja's tiki-taka revival on full display.
content:
Spain's footballing philosophy has always been rooted in control: control of the ball, control of space, control of the opponent's will to play. At SoFi Stadium on Tuesday evening, that philosophy was executed to near-perfection as a Pedri-inspired La Roja dismantled Germany 2-0 in the standout fixture of Group B. Luis de la Fuente's side may have looked vulnerable on the counter in patches, but for long stretches of this contest they played the kind of football that prompted comparisons to the immortal tiki-taka sides of 2008–2012.

Pedri pulls the strings

The Barcelona midfielder was everywhere: ghosting into pockets of space, recycling possession with one and two touches, and pressing with a tenacity that belied his slight frame. His first goal — a perfectly timed run onto Fabian Ruiz's reverse pass and a dinked finish over Manuel Neuer — came on 34 minutes and drew an audible gasp of appreciation from a genuinely neutral crowd. Germany looked stunned. They had controlled the early exchanges through Florian Wirtz and Jamal Musiala, but once Pedri found his rhythm, the entire Spanish midfield machine accelerated, and Germany's build-up was snuffed out at source time and again.

Germany's structural problem

Hansi Flick's side set up in a 4-2-3-1, but the two holding midfielders — Leon Goretzka and Emre Can — struggled to cope with Spain's movement. Whenever Germany advanced the ball to Wirtz or Musiala, Rodri would appear to intercept; whenever the wide forwards looked to drive, Spain's wing-backs had already tracked back. Musiala did create a golden opportunity just after the hour mark, cutting inside onto his left foot and curling an effort that came back off the post — the moment that, had it gone in, might have made this a very different contest.

Lamine Yamal's star shines

If Pedri provided the brains, 18-year-old Lamine Yamal provided the electricity. His assist for Pedri's second goal on 77 minutes — a nutmeg on Tah followed by a low cross cut back from the byline — was one of the individual moments of the tournament so far. Yamal has been exceptional throughout the competition, and Germany simply could not find a solution to his directness on the right flank. Antonio Rüdiger, one of the best defenders in the world, looked uncharacteristically nervous whenever Yamal received the ball in wide areas.

Numbers to admire

Spain completed 748 passes at an accuracy rate of 92%, compared to Germany's 412 at 81%. They created five clear-cut chances to Germany's two. Rodri won 11 of 13 duels and completed all three of his attempted long balls. These are not statistics that flatter to deceive; they are the fingerprints of a side playing at the height of their powers. Spain have now scored six goals and conceded none in two Group B matches and will advance to the last sixteen regardless of their result against Japan in the final round.

This performance will worry every side left in the tournament. Unlike the Spain of the late-Guardiola tiki-taka era, which was sometimes accused of sterile possession, this vintage combines technical brilliance with genuine attacking directness. If Pedri and Yamal remain fit and in this form, Spain may well be the side everyone else is trying to avoid in the knockout rounds.
